class.name: NetwEntityIds
class.brief_description: The process-wide mint every entity handle comes from.
class.description: An entity is constructed, configured and read long before a session exists to number it, so the mint cannot belong to one. It is process-wide and has no instance: every verb here is a static over one mint, because a wrapper that carries a handle from birth needs one no session owns. [NetwEntity] takes a handle here at construction and carries it for the whole life of the wrapper, and a session's [NetwLivenessCore] adopts that handle rather than owning it. That separation makes two questions different that used to be one. [method is_minted] asks whether a handle was ever issued, and [method NetwLivenessCore.entity_is_valid] asks whether one particular session knows the entity behind it. A handle from another session is minted and unknown, a handle from nowhere is neither, and a plane that cannot tell those apart answers the same refusal to a stale lookup and to a forged one. [codeblock] var handle := NetwEntityIds.mint() # one holder, the caller NetwEntityIds.retain(handle) # a second holder NetwEntityIds.release(handle) # still held NetwEntityIds.release(handle) # freed here, and never reissued [/codeblock] A handle has holders rather than an owner, because they end on different cadences: the engine finalizes a wrapper, and a record plane lets go at [method NetwLivenessCore.clear]. The value survives until the last holder releases, which is what lets a session tear down without stranding a wrapper that still holds. Released values are never issued again, so a late message naming a retired entity resolves to nothing rather than to whoever came next. Nothing in a game calls these. Reach for them only when writing the identity plane itself. The mint outlives every session, so the extension releases whatever is still outstanding at its own shutdown. A count read at process exit is therefore a session that failed to clear rather than the mint leaking.

method.name: holders
method.description: Returns how many holders [param entity] has, or [code]0[/code] when it names nothing. Exists so the last-holder rule is checkable rather than inferred from [method outstanding].

method.name: is_minted
method.description: Returns [code]true[/code] while [param entity] is a handle this mint issued and has not freed. Says nothing about whether any session knows the entity behind it.

method.name: mint
method.description: Returns a fresh handle with one holder, the caller. The caller owes it one [method release].

method.name: outstanding
method.description: Returns how many handles are still held. Exists so a teardown can be checked for having actually torn down.

method.name: release
method.description: Drops one hold on [param entity]. The last one frees the value. A handle this mint never issued is ignored.

method.name: retain
method.description: Claims another hold on [param entity], answering [code]false[/code] for a handle the mint never issued so an adoption cannot forge one.
